intro: When you feel sick, who helps you? Maybe a nurse, a doctor or a pharmacist. Around the world, people have asked the same question for thousands of years. They have built different ways of healing.

In this unit you will meet healers from the West, like Hippocrates, Florence Nightingale, Louis Pasteur and Clara Barton. You will also learn about Traditional Chinese Medicine from China and Ayurveda from India. Each tradition has its own ideas about the body.

You will see how science tests what works and what is safe. By the end, you will be able to compare traditions with respect. You will also know why it helps to tell your doctor about everything you use.
bigQuestion: How have people in different parts of the world cared for the sick, and how do we find out what really helps?

title: Medicine East and West

chapters.title: Doctors of the West
chapters.bigQuestion: How did people in the West learn what really makes us sick and what helps us get well?

story.title: The Lady with the Lamp
story.kicker: In a crowded army hospital, one nurse walks the halls at night and starts counting.
paragraphs: It is 1854. The place is Scutari, across the water from the city now called Istanbul. A huge army hospital sits on a hill. Inside, British soldiers from the Crimean War lie in long rows. The halls are dark and cold.

A nurse named Florence Nightingale carries a small lamp. She walks the long halls late at night. She stops at each bed. She speaks softly to the men. The soldiers start to call her the Lady with the Lamp.

Florence sees more than sick men. She sees dirty floors and dirty sheets. She smells bad air. She sees that the water is not clean. Many soldiers are not dying from their wounds. They are dying from sickness that spreads inside the hospital.

So Florence does something new. She counts. She writes down who gets sick and who dies. She and her nurses scrub, wash and bring in clean food. Later she uses her numbers to show leaders that clean hospitals save lives.
story.think: Florence carried a lamp, but she also carried a notebook. Why might counting be just as important as caring?

lessons.title: Hippocrates Looks Closely
lessons.mainIdea: Hippocrates of ancient Greece taught that illness has natural causes that doctors can watch and study.
reading: About 2,400 years ago, a doctor named Hippocrates lived on the Greek island of Kos. Many people then believed that angry gods sent sickness. A sick person might pray at a temple and hope to be healed.

Hippocrates and his students had a different idea. They taught that illness has *natural causes*. Food, water, weather and the way a person lives can all play a part. That means a doctor can look for the cause.

So Hippocrates watched his patients closely. He wrote down their fever, breathing and sleep day by day. This careful watching is called *observation*. Doctors still start the same way today. They look, listen and ask questions.

words.d: reasons for something that come from the world around us, not from magic or gods
watching something carefully and noting what you see

look.title: A Doctor's Notebook
look.text: Picture a doctor in ancient Greece. A boy has a fever. The doctor does not guess. He writes: Day 1, hot skin, no hunger. Day 2, still hot, coughing. Day 3, cooler, eating a little. He reads his notes to see how the boy is changing.
look.prompt: What can the doctor learn from notes that he could not learn from one quick look?

check.q: Where did Hippocrates live?
choices: On the Greek island of Kos
In Rome during the Middle Ages
check.why: The reading says Hippocrates lived on the Greek island of Kos, about 2,400 years ago.

check.q: What big idea did Hippocrates teach about illness?
choices: Illness is always sent by angry gods
Illness only comes from bad luck
check.why: Hippocrates taught that illness has natural causes, like food, water and weather.

check.q: What is observation?
choices: Watching carefully and noting what you see
check.why: Observation means watching carefully. Hippocrates wrote down what he saw each day.

lessons.title: The Four Humors
lessons.mainIdea: For about 2,000 years, doctors believed in four humors, until science replaced that idea.
reading: Greek doctors tried to explain why people got sick. They taught that the body holds four fluids, called the four *humors*. They were blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. Health meant the four were in balance.

Doctors in Europe and the Middle East believed this for about 2,000 years. To fix a fever, a doctor might take blood out of a sick person. This was called bleeding. We now know it often made people weaker.

Then scientists looked more closely. They used microscopes and careful tests. They found germs and learned how organs work. The humor idea was replaced. This is how *science* works. When new evidence comes, ideas can change.

words.d: four body fluids that old Greek doctors believed had to stay in balance
a way of learning about the world by watching, testing and checking evidence

look.title: Two Doctors, Two Ideas
look.text: Doctor A, long ago: This man has a fever. He has too much blood. I will take some out. Doctor B, today: This man has a fever. I will test his blood for germs. Then I will choose a medicine that tests have shown works.
look.prompt: How does Doctor B decide what to do? How is that different from Doctor A?

check.q: How many humors did the old Greek doctors describe?
check.why: They described four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile.

check.q: About how long did people believe in the four humors?
check.why: The reading says doctors believed in the humors for about 2,000 years.

check.q: Why was the humor idea replaced?
choices: A king made a new law
New evidence showed germs and how organs work
check.why: Microscopes and careful tests gave new evidence. In science, ideas change when evidence changes.

lessons.title: A Promise to Patients
lessons.mainIdea: The Hippocratic Oath is an old promise that doctors will help the sick and not harm them.
reading: When new doctors finish school, many stand up and make a promise out loud. The oldest famous promise for doctors is the *Hippocratic Oath*. It is named for Hippocrates. His followers probably wrote it.

An *oath* is a serious promise. In the old oath, a doctor promises to help the sick as well as he can. He promises not to hurt them on purpose. He also promises to keep private what patients tell him.
Today many medical schools use newer promises. The words have changed over time. But the main ideas stay the same. Help the patient. Do no harm. Keep the patient's secrets safe.

words.d: a serious promise, often said out loud in front of others
an old Greek promise for doctors, named after Hippocrates

look.title: From the Hippocratic Oath
look.text: I will use treatment to help the sick as well as I am able and as I judge best. I will never use it to hurt or wrong anyone.
look.cite: Hippocratic Oath, ancient Greece, about 400 BCE (paraphrased in plain words)
look.prompt: Which part of this promise matches the idea do no harm?

check.q: What is an oath?
check.why: An oath is a serious promise, often said out loud.

check.q: Who probably wrote the Hippocratic Oath?
check.why: The reading says the oath is named for Hippocrates, but his followers probably wrote it.

check.q: Which is one of the main ideas of the oath?
check.why: The oath promises to help the sick and not hurt them. Do no harm is a main idea.

lessons.title: Nightingale Cleans Up
lessons.mainIdea: Florence Nightingale showed that clean, airy hospitals help sick people get well.
reading: Florence Nightingale was born in 1820 to a rich English family. She wanted to be a nurse. Her family did not like the idea. In those days nursing was not a respected job. Florence did it anyway.

In 1854 she led a group of nurses to the army hospital at Scutari. She saw dirt, bad air and crowded beds. Her team scrubbed floors, washed sheets and cooked healthy food. They opened windows for fresh air. Good *sanitation*, or keeping places clean, became her goal.
Back home, Florence wrote a famous book called Notes on Nursing in 1859. In 1860 she started a school to train nurses in London. She helped make *nursing* a skilled and respected job.

words.d: keeping places clean, with clean water and safe ways to remove waste
the job of caring for sick or hurt people and helping them stay well

look.title: Nightingale's First Rule
look.text: It may seem a strange principle to enunciate as the very first requirement in a Hospital that it should do the sick no harm.
look.cite: Florence Nightingale, Notes on Hospitals, 3rd edition, 1863
look.prompt: Nightingale says a hospital should do the sick no harm. How could a dirty hospital harm a patient?

check.q: Where did Florence Nightingale lead nurses in 1854?
check.why: In 1854 she led nurses to the army hospital at Scutari during the Crimean War.

check.q: What does sanitation mean?
choices: Keeping places clean with clean water
check.why: Sanitation means keeping places clean, with clean water and safe ways to remove waste.

check.q: What did Nightingale start in London in 1860?
check.why: In 1860 she started a school to train nurses in London.

lessons.title: Counting Saves Lives
lessons.mainIdea: Nightingale used numbers and charts to prove that clean hospitals save lives.
reading: Florence Nightingale loved math. At Scutari she kept careful records. She wrote down how many soldiers died each month. She also wrote down why they died.

Her numbers showed something surprising. Far more soldiers died from sicknesses like cholera and typhus than from battle wounds. Many of these sicknesses spread through dirty water and crowded rooms. Cleaning up could prevent them.

Leaders were busy and did not like long reports. So Florence drew colorful charts. Each wedge showed deaths in one month. The charts made the problem easy to see. This kind of number evidence is called *data*. Her data helped change army hospitals.

words.d: facts and numbers collected to learn something
written notes kept over time about what happened

look.title: Reading a Chart
look.text: Picture a round chart like a pie. Each slice is one month. Blue shading shows deaths from sickness. Red shading shows deaths from wounds. In most months, the blue part is much bigger than the red part.
look.prompt: What would a leader learn from seeing that the blue part is bigger?

check.q: What did Nightingale's numbers show?
choices: More soldiers died from sickness than from wounds
check.why: Her records showed that sicknesses like cholera and typhus killed more soldiers than wounds.

check.q: Why did Nightingale draw charts?
choices: To make the problem easy for leaders to see
check.why: Leaders did not like long reports. Her charts made the problem easy to see.

check.q: What is data?
choices: Facts and numbers collected to learn something
check.why: Data means facts and numbers collected to learn something, like Nightingale's records.

lessons.title: Pasteur Finds Germs
lessons.mainIdea: Louis Pasteur showed that tiny living germs cause spoiling and many diseases.
reading: In France in the 1860s, a scientist named Louis Pasteur studied why milk and wine go bad. He looked through a microscope. He saw tiny living things too small to see with your eyes. We call them *germs*, or microbes.

Pasteur did a famous test. He boiled broth in flasks with long curved necks. Dust and germs from the air got stuck in the curve. The broth stayed fresh. When germs got in, the broth spoiled. Germs came from other germs, not from nothing.

Pasteur found that heating milk kills many harmful germs. This is called *pasteurization*, after him. He also helped make vaccines. His work led to *germ theory*, the idea that germs cause many diseases.

words.d: tiny living things, too small to see, that can make people sick
heating a food like milk to kill harmful germs
the idea that many diseases are caused by germs

look.title: The Swan-Neck Flask
look.text: Two flasks hold boiled broth. Flask A has a long neck that curves down like a swan's neck. Air gets in, but dust gets stuck in the curve. Flask B has a short, straight neck. Dust falls right in. After a few days, the broth in Flask B is cloudy. Flask A stays clear.
look.prompt: Why did the broth in Flask B spoil, but not the broth in Flask A?

check.q: Where did Louis Pasteur do his work?
check.why: The reading says Pasteur worked in France in the 1860s.

check.q: What is pasteurization?
choices: Heating milk to kill harmful germs
check.why: Pasteurization means heating a food like milk to kill harmful germs. It is named after Pasteur.

check.q: What does germ theory say?
choices: Many diseases are caused by germs
check.why: Germ theory is the idea that germs cause many diseases.

lessons.title: Clara Barton Helps
lessons.mainIdea: Clara Barton cared for soldiers and founded the American Red Cross in 1881.
reading: Clara Barton was born in Massachusetts in 1821. During the American Civil War she brought food, bandages and medicine right to the battlefields. She cared for hurt soldiers. People called her the Angel of the Battlefield.

After the war, Clara visited Europe. There she learned about the International Red Cross. It helped people hurt in war. Clara wanted the same help in America. In 1881 she founded the *American Red Cross*.

The Red Cross also helps after *disasters* like floods, fires and storms. It gives shelter, food and first aid. Today it also collects donated blood for hospitals. Clara showed that one person can start help that lasts.

words.d: a group, founded by Clara Barton in 1881, that helps people in wars and disasters
sudden events like floods, fires or storms that cause great harm

look.title: After the Storm
look.text: A big storm has knocked down trees. A family's house is flooded. Volunteers in red and white vests set up cots in a school gym. They hand out water, blankets and hot meals. A nurse checks a boy's scraped knee.
look.prompt: Which of these helpers' jobs connect to what Clara Barton started?

check.q: What did people call Clara Barton?
check.why: Soldiers called Clara Barton the Angel of the Battlefield. The Lady with the Lamp was Nightingale.

check.q: In what year did Clara Barton found the American Red Cross?
check.why: The reading says she founded the American Red Cross in 1881.

check.q: What does the Red Cross do after disasters?
choices: Gives shelter, food and first aid
check.why: After floods, fires and storms, the Red Cross gives shelter, food and first aid.

lessons.title: Hospitals, Labs and Medicines
lessons.mainIdea: Today doctors, nurses, labs and tested medicines work together to help people heal.
reading: Imagine a girl with a bad sore throat. A doctor looks at her throat. A nurse gently swabs it. The swab goes to a *laboratory*, or lab. A worker there tests it for a kind of germ called strep bacteria.

The test comes back positive. The doctor gives an *antibiotic*. Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria. In 1928 Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin, one of the first antibiotics. Antibiotics do not work on viruses, like a cold.
A pharmacist fills the medicine and explains how to take it. Many people work as a team. Always take medicine only the way a doctor or pharmacist says. Ask a trusted adult if you have questions.

words.d: a room where people run tests and do science, often called a lab
a medicine that kills bacteria or stops them from growing
a trained person who prepares medicines and explains how to use them safely

look.title: Living Longer in the U.S.
look.cite: National Center for Health Statistics (CDC), U.S. life expectancy data
look.prompt: How many more years did people live on average in 2000 than in 1900? What changes in medicine might help explain this?

check.q: What does an antibiotic do?
check.why: Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop them from growing. They do not work on viruses like a cold.

check.q: Who discovered penicillin in 1928?
check.why: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928.

check.q: Who fills medicine and explains how to take it?
check.why: A pharmacist prepares medicines and explains how to use them safely.

lessons.title: Testing What Works
lessons.mainIdea: Scientists test medicines on groups of people to find out if they are safe and if they work.
reading: Suppose a company makes a new medicine for headaches. How do we know it works? People might feel better anyway. So scientists run a fair test called a *clinical trial*.

In a trial, volunteers are split into two groups by chance. One group gets the new medicine. The other group gets a *placebo*, a pill with no medicine in it. Nobody in the groups knows which one they got. Then scientists compare the two groups.

Trials start small, with a few people, to check safety. Then they grow bigger. Only after many tests can a medicine be sold. In the U.S., the Food and Drug Administration, or FDA, checks the results. This is science testing what works.

words.d: a careful test of a medicine or treatment with volunteers
a pretend pill or treatment with no medicine in it, used to compare in a test

look.title: Trials Get Bigger
look.unit: people in a typical trial phase
look.cite: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, The Drug Development Process, Step 3: Clinical Research
look.prompt: Why do you think trials start with few people and end with thousands?

check.q: What is a placebo?
choices: A pill with no medicine in it
check.why: A placebo has no medicine in it. It lets scientists compare it with the real medicine.

check.q: Why do scientists compare two groups in a trial?
choices: To see if the medicine helps more than a placebo
To make the test take longer
Because one group is always sick
check.why: Comparing groups shows whether people improve because of the medicine or would have gotten better anyway.

check.q: Which U.S. agency checks trial results?
check.why: In the U.S., the Food and Drug Administration, or FDA, checks the results.

review.q: Which person taught that illness has natural causes?
review.why: Hippocrates of ancient Greece taught that illness has natural causes.

review.q: What does the four humors story show about science?
choices: Ideas can change when new evidence comes
review.why: The humor idea was believed for 2,000 years, then replaced when new evidence came.

review.q: Who was called the Lady with the Lamp?
review.why: Florence Nightingale walked the dark wards with a lamp at Scutari.

choices: She showed them data and charts
review.why: Nightingale kept records and drew charts that made the problem easy to see.

review.q: What did Pasteur's swan-neck flask test show?
choices: Germs come from other germs, not from nothing
review.why: Broth stayed fresh when germs could not get in. Germs come from other germs.

review.q: How are Nightingale and Clara Barton alike?
choices: Both cared for soldiers and started lasting work
review.why: Both cared for soldiers in war and started lasting work: nurse training and the American Red Cross.

review.q: A friend has a cold, caused by a virus. Will an antibiotic kill it?
choices: No, antibiotics do not work on viruses
review.why: Antibiotics kill bacteria. They do not work on viruses like a cold.

choices: A careful test of a medicine with volunteers
review.why: A clinical trial is a fair test of a medicine or treatment with volunteers.

chapters.title: Traditional Chinese Medicine and Ayurveda
chapters.bigQuestion: How do very old healing traditions from China and India see the body, and what does science find when it studies them?

story.title: Two Visits in One Week
story.kicker: A boy watches two very different healers and notices something they share.
paragraphs: On Tuesday, Wei goes with his grandmother to her acupuncturist. The room is quiet and smells like tea. Dr. Lin asks Grandma how she sleeps and what she eats. She looks at Grandma's tongue. She holds Grandma's wrist for a long time and feels her pulse.

Then Dr. Lin places a few needles, thinner than a hair, in Grandma's arms and legs. Grandma rests with her eyes closed. Wei is surprised. Grandma says it does not hurt. She says it helps her sore knee feel better.

On Friday, Wei has a checkup with his pediatrician, Dr. Brooks. She asks how he sleeps and what he eats. She looks in his throat. She presses two fingers on his wrist to count his pulse. She listens to his heart with a stethoscope.

On the way home, Wei thinks hard. The two doctors used different ideas and different tools. But both asked questions. Both looked closely. Both checked his pulse. Both wanted the person in front of them to feel well.
At dinner, Wei tells Grandma what he noticed. Grandma smiles. She says she tells Dr. Brooks about her acupuncture and her herbs, too. That way, all her helpers can work together.
story.think: What did both of Wei's doctors do? Why is it important for Grandma to tell each doctor what the other does?

lessons.title: Qi, Yin and Yang
lessons.mainIdea: Traditional Chinese Medicine teaches that health comes from balance and the smooth flow of qi.
reading: *Traditional Chinese Medicine*, or TCM, began in China thousands of years ago. A famous old book, The Yellow Emperor's Classic of Internal Medicine, was put together about 2,000 years ago. Millions of people use TCM today.

TCM teaches about *qi*, said like chee. In TCM, qi is a life energy that flows through the body. TCM teaches that qi moves along paths called meridians. When qi flows smoothly, TCM says, a person is healthy.

TCM also teaches about *yin and yang*. These are two opposite sides that need each other, like cool and warm or rest and action. TCM says health comes from their balance. These are the tradition's ideas. Scientists have not measured qi or meridians.

words.d: a very old system of healing from China, often called TCM
in TCM, a life energy that the tradition teaches flows through the body
in Chinese thought, two opposite sides, like cool and warm, that need to be in balance

look.title: Opposites in Balance
look.text: Think about a day. Morning is bright and busy. Night is dark and quiet. You need both. If you never rested, you would be worn out. If you never moved, you would feel stiff. Chinese thought calls this kind of pair yin and yang.
look.prompt: Name another pair of opposites in your own day that need to be in balance.

check.q: In TCM, what is qi?
choices: A life energy the tradition says flows through the body
A germ seen in a microscope
check.why: TCM teaches that qi is a life energy that flows through the body along meridians.

check.q: What are yin and yang?
choices: Two opposite sides that need balance
check.why: Yin and yang are opposite sides, like cool and warm, that TCM says must be in balance.

check.q: What does the reading say scientists have found about qi?
choices: They see it in every x-ray
They proved it is a germ
They have not measured qi or meridians
check.why: The reading says qi and meridians are the tradition's ideas. Scientists have not measured them.

lessons.title: Thin Needles
lessons.mainIdea: Acupuncture uses very thin needles, and studies show it may help some kinds of pain for some people.
reading: Remember Wei's grandmother. Her healer placed very thin needles in her skin. This is called *acupuncture*. It is one of the best-known parts of TCM. The needles are much thinner than a needle for a shot.
TCM teaches that the needles go into special points, called acupuncture points. The tradition says this helps qi flow. A trained, licensed acupuncturist uses clean needles that are used only once.

Scientists have studied acupuncture in many tests. Some studies show it may help some people with certain kinds of pain, like low back pain or sore knees. For many other problems the evidence is unclear. Scientists still study how and why it helps.

words.d: a practice from TCM where very thin needles are placed at certain points on the body
facts from tests and observations that show whether something is true

look.title: What Researchers Say
look.text: Acupuncture may help ease some kinds of pain, such as low back pain, neck pain and knee pain from arthritis. For many other conditions, the research is less clear.
look.cite: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH), Acupuncture: What You Need To Know (paraphrased)
look.prompt: What kinds of pain does this say acupuncture may help? What does it say about other problems?

check.q: What does an acupuncturist use?
check.why: Acupuncture uses very thin needles placed at certain points.

check.q: What do studies say about acupuncture and pain?
choices: It may help some kinds of pain for some people
check.why: Studies show it may help some kinds of pain, like low back pain. For many other problems the evidence is unclear.

check.q: Why does a licensed acupuncturist use needles only once?
choices: To keep things clean and safe
check.why: Clean needles used only once help keep patients safe.

lessons.title: Herbs and Moving Slowly
lessons.mainIdea: TCM uses herbs and gentle movement like tai chi and qigong, and tai chi can help balance.
reading: Early one morning in a park, a group of older adults moves slowly together. They shift their weight and turn their arms like flowing water. This is *tai chi*. A similar practice with breathing and gentle moves is called *qigong*.

Studies show that tai chi can help older adults improve their balance. Better balance means fewer falls. It can also help people feel calm. Many community centers in the U.S. now offer tai chi classes.

TCM also uses *herbal medicine*, made from roots, leaves and bark. One plant from Chinese tradition, sweet wormwood, led scientist Tu Youyou to a malaria medicine. She won a Nobel Prize in 2015. But herbs can be strong. Always tell your doctor about any herbs you take.

words.d: a slow, flowing exercise from China that helps with balance and calm
a Chinese practice that joins gentle movement with slow breathing
remedies made from plants, such as roots, leaves and bark

look.title: Try It Slowly
look.text: Stand up tall. Put your weight on your left foot. Slowly lift your right heel. Now shift your weight to the right foot, very slowly, like pouring honey. Breathe in as you shift one way. Breathe out as you shift back.
look.prompt: How did moving slowly feel? Why might practicing this help a person keep their balance?

check.q: What can tai chi help older adults do?
check.why: Studies show tai chi can help older adults improve balance and fall less.

check.q: What is qigong?
choices: Gentle movement joined with slow breathing
check.why: Qigong joins gentle movement with slow breathing.

check.q: Why should you tell your doctor about herbs you take?
choices: Herbs can be strong and can mix with other medicines
check.why: Herbs can be strong. Your doctor needs to know everything you take to keep you safe.

lessons.title: The Science of Life
lessons.mainIdea: Ayurveda is an old healing tradition from India that teaches about three doshas in balance.
reading: *Ayurveda* comes from India. Its name means knowledge of life. Old books of Ayurveda, like the Charaka Samhita, are about 2,000 years old. Many millions of people in India and around the world still use it.

Ayurveda holds that each person has a mix of three *doshas*. They are named vata, pitta and kapha. Ayurveda links vata with air and movement, pitta with fire and digestion, and kapha with earth, water and steadiness.

Ayurveda teaches that every person has their own mix. It says health comes when the doshas are in balance. These are the tradition's ideas. Science has not measured doshas the way it measures blood pressure.

words.d: a very old healing tradition from India whose name means knowledge of life
in Ayurveda, the three forces, vata, pitta and kapha, said to shape each person

look.title: Three Doshas in Ayurveda
look.text: Vata: Ayurveda links it to air and movement, like wind. Pitta: Ayurveda links it to fire and heat, like the energy that digests food. Kapha: Ayurveda links it to earth and water, like strong, steady ground.
look.prompt: How is the idea of three doshas in balance like the idea of yin and yang in balance? How is it different?

lessons.title: Yoga and Breathing
lessons.mainIdea: Yoga comes from India and can help with stretching, strength and feeling calm.
reading: In a school gym, a class sits on mats. The teacher says, breathe in slowly, now breathe out. The students stretch their arms up like a tall tree. This is *yoga*. Yoga began in India long ago and is closely linked with Ayurveda.
Yoga joins body poses, slow *breathing* and quiet focus. Some poses stretch. Some build strength. Slow breathing can help a busy mind feel calmer. You can do it anywhere.

Studies show yoga can help people stretch, get stronger and feel less stressed. For some adults, it may help low back pain. Yoga does not cure serious diseases. Start slowly, and stop if something hurts.

words.d: a practice from India that joins body poses, breathing and quiet focus
moving air in and out of your lungs; slow breathing can help you feel calm

lessons.title: Food and Spices
lessons.mainIdea: Ayurveda uses food and spices for balance, and some remedies need care because they may not be tested or clean.
reading: Ayurveda pays close attention to *diet*, the food a person eats. It teaches that warm, fresh meals help balance. Spices like ginger, cumin and turmeric are common in Ayurvedic cooking.

Turmeric is a yellow spice. It gives curry its bright color. Scientists are studying turmeric. So far there is not strong evidence that it treats diseases. Enjoying it in food is common and usually safe.

Some Ayurvedic *supplements* sold as pills have been tested by scientists. In a 2008 study, some products bought online contained lead or mercury. These metals can harm the body. So buy only with a trusted adult, and tell your doctor about anything you take.

words.d: the food and drink a person usually has
pills or powders people take in addition to food, such as herbs or vitamins

lessons.title: Used by Millions
lessons.mainIdea: Traditional medicine is used in most countries in the world, so it matters to study it carefully.
reading: Walk down a street in Chicago's Chinatown and you may see a shop with jars of dried roots and herbs. Traditional medicine is part of life for many families around the world.

The World Health Organization, or WHO, is a group that works on health for the whole world. In a 2019 report, WHO said that most of its member countries report that people there use *traditional medicine*.

Because so many people use these traditions, it matters to know what is safe and what helps. Some countries now train and license traditional healers. They also check that herbs are clean and labeled.

words.d: healing practices passed down over many generations in a culture
a group of the United Nations that works on health around the world, called WHO

lessons.title: How Scientists Test
lessons.mainIdea: Scientists test traditional practices with fair tests, and results show some help and some do not.
reading: Scientists test traditional practices the same way they test new medicines. They use fair tests, like clinical trials. One group tries the practice. Another group does not. Then they compare.

Some results are clear. Tai chi helps older adults with balance. Yoga helps with stretching and feeling calm. Acupuncture may help some kinds of pain. Tu Youyou's work with sweet wormwood led to a malaria medicine used around the world.

Other results are unclear, or show no help. Some remedies may even cause harm. That is why scientists keep testing. Good science asks: does it help, for whom, and is it safe? The answer is not always the same for every practice.

words.d: a test where only one thing is changed so results can be compared
what a test shows when it is finished

lessons.title: One Team for Your Health
lessons.mainIdea: Tell your doctor about everything you use, so all your helpers can work together safely.
reading: Remember Wei's grandmother. She sees an acupuncturist and a regular doctor. She tells both of them what the other does. This helps keep her safe. Her helpers act as one *health care team*.
Some herbs can change how other medicines work. A doctor or *pharmacist* can check whether things are safe to take together. They can only help if they know what you use.

You can help your own health, too. Tell a parent or trusted adult when you feel sick. Help your family make a list of any medicines, herbs or supplements. Bring the list to checkups. Asking questions is a smart and brave thing to do.

words.d: all the people who help care for your health, working together
a trained person who prepares medicines and checks that they are safe to take together
